title: Liudprand of Cremona: a people once “unknown to all of us”
fact_summary: Writing around 960, Liudprand says the Hungarians, whose savagery almost every nation had felt, had once been unknown in the West, shut off behind barriers the common people called “clusae”.

place.label: The passage names no place; where Liudprand wrote is not fixed in the sources read so far

claims.text: Liudprand writes: “Ungariorum gens, cuius omnes poene nationes expertae sunt saevitiam … nobis omnibus tunc temporis habebatur ignota”, that is, the Hungarian people, whose savagery almost all nations have experienced, was at that time unknown to all of us.
claims.certainty_reason: This records what the source says. The passage was read in Latin in the open copy linked under Sources.

claims.text: He explains that they were separated “by certain very troublesome barriers, which the common people call clusae”, so that they could go out neither to the south nor to the west.
claims.certainty_reason: This records what the source says. The passage was read in Latin in the open copy linked under Sources.

claims.text: In the same sentence he says that now, terrified by the power of King Otto, they “do not dare even to whisper”.
claims.certainty_reason: This records what the source says. The passage was read in Latin in the open copy linked under Sources.

dating_methods.text: The database dates the period this passage describes to 870–887, and the writing of the Antapodosis to 958–962. The passage itself gives no year.
dating_methods.certainty_reason: The period is the database editors' reading of where the passage sits in the narrative.

open_questions.text: Which barriers did Liudprand mean by “clusae”: mountain passes, or defences built against the Hungarians?
